newsitem.title: USA: WORLD BONDS - BTPs to survive late Italian EMU entry.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - BTPs to survive late Italian EMU entry.

text.p: Italian bonds righted themselves and are on course for further strengthening, after taking a broadside from reports of a possible delay in Italy's joining Europe's single currency.
Still, their performance this year may not match recent stellar gains, global strategists said.

"The best is over, but it doesn't look to me like lira bonds are going to get hammered, independent of whether they (Italy) are in or out," said Alan Ruskin, research director at I.D.E.A., an international market consulting firm.

Italian BTPs were jostled along with the lira and have see-sawed this week since a story in the Financial Times said the European Union would offer Italy a face-saving deal that would postpone its entry into Eurpoean Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) for up to 18 months.
The report prompted profit-taking as investors moved to protect lucrative bets that high Italian interest rates would converge with Germany's in time for EMU's scheduled launch date in 1999.

The plan, as reported in the British paper, would take into account Germany's fears that Italy's participation in the first round of EMU would threaten the status of the proposed euro as a strong currency.
But international bond experts said Italy would likely make continued headway in meeting the fiscal and economic conditions for joining, regardless of the timetable.

"As long as Italy's commitment towards EMU is intact, it doesn't really matter whether it is in in 1999 or 2001," said Ben Ghalmi, vice president and analyst for European fixed income markets at Alliance Capital Management Corp.

Perhaps the biggest benefactor of the uncertainty surrounding Italy this week was the British pound, which surged as investors flocked to the relative safety and high yields of investments in the gilt market.

"If we're not at cycle highs, we're close to a cycle high and (the gilt market) is seen as something of a safe haven from EMU turmoil," said Richard Koss, an international strategist at MFR Inc, an investment advisory firm.
Koss said the Italian bond market is subject to additional profit-taking.

With yields on 10-year Italian bonds at virtually the same level as 10-year gilts -- which at just under 7.2 percent offer a 150-basis-point premium over German bunds -- he said he would place his bets in Britain, where 10-year interest rates have room to fall below 7.0 percent.

"I'm not damning the U.K. with faint praise, but given a choice between them and the Italians, I'm not sure there is as much room for gains as there is in the U.K., particularly since there is still a lot of this convergence money in the Italian play that could come out in a volatile manner," Koss said.
Perversely, during the BTP rally, Italian interest rates converged through par, to stand under those of Britain, before the recent gilt rally, analysts said.

Not that long ago, when Italian yields stood near 7.0 percent, 10-year gilts were yielding about 7.6 percent, Ruskin noted. But he thinks the latest bets on Britain-Italy convergence have reached their maximum potential.
"One has seen a kind of lira-sterling switch, i.e., out of lira into sterling. I think that has largely run its course," he said.

Meanwhile, with Italy still in a contractionary budget-slashing mode before eventually joining EMU, the country will probably need to keep its economy on track with ongoing stimulation on the monetary side, strategists predicted.
Ruskin said this would keep demand for Italian investments well supported, especially at the short end of the BTP curve.
